newsitem.title: GERMANY: German prosecutors absolve banks as tycoon charged.
newsitem.headline: German prosecutors absolve banks as tycoon charged.

text.p: Prosecutors probing one of Germany's biggest corporate scandals said on Monday they had charged tycoon Juergen Schneider with fraud while finding no evidence to back allegations that his banks were to blame.
Outlining charges against the disgraced entrepreneur, the Frankfurt prosecutors' office said Schneider duped banks into extending credit by overstating rent income and forging bills.

Schneider, whose property empire collapsed under more than five billion marks ($3.19 billion) of debt in 1994, has been charged with credit fraud, serious fraud and a bankruptcy offence. The charges could put him in jail for up to 15 years.
But prosecutors said they had found no evidence of any wrongdoing by banks, contrary to repeated claims by Schneider that his creditors sabotaged him.
"In the investigation so far we have found no indications that criminal acts were conducted in the banks," Frankfurt prosecutor Dieter Haike told a news conference.
"But mistakes were made. There is no such thing as an infallible examination of creditworthiness."

The Schneider bankruptcy in 1994 sparked fears of a German real estate slump, left hundreds of small craftsmen fighting for their livelihoods and exposed Schneider's banks to public outrage at the apparent ease with which he obtained funding.

Deutsche Bank, which bore the brunt of criticism for loose lending and lax supervision, later that year accepted the resignation of four executives as a result of the debacle. But it maintained they had not behaved dishonourably.

Deutsche, Schneider's largest creditor, made matters worse for itself when its chief executive Hilmar Kopper dismissed as "peanuts" the millions of marks Schneider owed to small tradesmen and builders.
On Monday, the bank declined official comment on the charges but said claims that it was responsible for the bankruptcy were "absurd."
"The victim is being turned into the culprit here," a spokesman said.
Schneider is being held in a local Frankfurt prison. If the Frankfurt district court approves the charges, the case is expected to go to trial this summer at the earliest.
Schneider's wife Claudia, who has been conditionally freed from detention because of concern for her health, has been charged with bankruptcy and two associates have been charged with helping him.
Schneider's Munich law firm could not be reached for comment on Monday. His lawyer Christoph Rueckel said on Sunday Schneider was committed to fighting the allegations.

Schneider, a bricklayer who became one of Germany's most celebrated entrepreneurs, gained fame by refurbishing historic hotels and stylish shopping malls in the post-unification property boom, adding flair to cities up and down the country.
But his facade crumbled as his rent income was too low to repay his debts, causing the group to slide towards bankruptcy.
He and his wife Claudia vanished in April 1994, sparking a year-long manhunt which ended with their arrest in Miami. They returned voluntarily to Germany last February.
Prosecutors said Schneider had provided them with substantial information in interviews they had conducted twice a week over the last three months.
"But Schneider did not concede that he made gave false information to banks," Heike said.
The instances of alleged fraud cited in the charges are against Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank AG, BHF-Bank AG, Norddeutsche Landesbank and Deutsche Bau- und Bodenbank AG.

In one case, in which Deutsche was allegedly defrauded of 45 million marks in 1992, Schneider is accused of having presented forged rental agreements to secure credit for the Zeilgalerie shopping mall in the centre of Frankfurt.
In another, Schneider allegedly caused 48 million marks worth of damage to Norddeutsche Landesbank by overstating the price he had paid to buy property in central Berlin.
The bankruptcy charge against Schneider alleges that he syphoned 245 million marks from his company and transferred the money to a Geneva account shortly before he fled the country.
